lesson.title: When the Machinery of Sleep Breaks Down
lesson.summary: Sleep disorders are persistent disruptions to the structure or timing of sleep, and understanding them requires knowing both how healthy sleep is organized into stages and what chronic sleep loss does to the body and mind.
lesson.body:
Every night the brain cycles through a predictable architecture of Sleep Stages: light NREM sleep, deep slow wave NREM sleep, and REM sleep, and each stage does different physiological and psychological work. A sleep disorder is a persistent problem with the amount, quality, or timing of sleep that prevents this architecture from unfolding normally, even when a person is given plenty of time in bed. This distinguishes a disorder from ordinary Sleep Deprivation, which usually results from simply not allotting enough hours to sleep. Someone with a sleep disorder can spend eight hours in bed and still wake up exhausted, because the problem is not the clock, it is the underlying process.

Insomnia, the most common sleep disorder, involves persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early and being unable to return to sleep. Because insomnia reduces total sleep time and fragments what sleep does occur, it produces the same downstream effects as chronic sleep deprivation: impaired attention, irritability, and slowed reaction time. Sleep apnea works differently. In obstructive sleep apnea, throat muscles relax enough during sleep to block the airway, so breathing repeatedly stops and the brain briefly rouses the sleeper to resume breathing, often many times a night without the person ever fully waking or remembering it. The person may believe they slept a full night, yet they never sustain the deeper stages of sleep, so they wake feeling as depleted as someone who barely slept at all.

Narcolepsy illustrates how a sleep disorder can involve stages intruding at the wrong time rather than being blocked. People with narcolepsy experience sudden, overwhelming sleep attacks during normal waking activity, and some also experience cataplexy, a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion like laughter or surprise. Cataplexy looks almost like the muscle paralysis that normally accompanies REM sleep, and that is essentially what it is: REM related atonia intruding into wakefulness. Narcolepsy has been linked to the loss of hypothalamic neurons that produce a neurotransmitter involved in maintaining stable wakefulness, which helps explain why the boundary between sleep and waking becomes unstable.

Parasomnias such as sleepwalking and night terrors occur during deep NREM slow wave sleep rather than REM, a useful detail for telling them apart from nightmares. A child having a night terror may sit up screaming with a racing heart and no memory of it the next morning, precisely because deep NREM sleep does not carry the vivid narrative dreaming associated with REM. Sleepwalking arises the same way, as the body partially rouses out of deep NREM sleep while consciousness lags behind.

Taken together, these disorders show why sleep science pays close attention to stages rather than just total hours. A disorder that fragments deep NREM sleep, intrudes REM atonia into waking, or simply shortens sleep overall will produce a familiar set of consequences: the same fatigue, cognitive fog, and mood disruption seen in ordinary sleep deprivation, because the underlying restorative processes are the ones being interrupted.
